title: Small Farm Ideas: What Can You Grow and Earn From on a Small Piece of Land?
metaTitle: Small Farm Ideas in the Philippines: What to Grow and Sell
metaDescription: Small farm ideas for Filipino growers: fast leafy greens and vegetables you pick for weeks, with days to harvest and a way to check real profit.
excerpt: The best small farm ideas in the Philippines are crops that grow fast, sell nearby and pay you more than once: leafy greens like pechay and mustasa, and fruiting vegetables like ampalaya, okra, sitaw and talong that you pick every few days. Choose by your water, your sun and your buyers, not by a viral video. anee.io, a farm app built for Filipino farmers, helps you plan the plot by date and keep the costs and sales that show whether it truly earns.

blocks.text:
A small piece of land can feed a family and still sell a surplus. But it cannot carry a mistake for long. A slow crop, a crop no one nearby buys, or a crop that needs more water than you have will eat a season's savings.

So the best ideas share three traits: they grow fast, they sell close to home, and they give more than one harvest. Below are the crops that fit, with their harvest times, and a way to check if your plot really earns.

items: Fast leafy greens turn cash quickly. Pechay can be harvested 30 to 40 days after sowing.
Fruiting vegetables pay over many pickings. Okra can be picked 40 to 45 times in one cropping season.
Your profit is sales minus every cost, including your own work days. Keep records from the first day.
The DA urban and peri urban agriculture program lists seeds, organic fertilizer and starter kits among its services.

blocks.text: What makes a good small farm idea?
Test every idea against these points before you spend. One weak point is a warning. Two is a no.

blocks.text: Which crops suit small farm ideas in the Philippines?
These lowland vegetables are common in the Philippines, and they are good to earn from when grown the right way. The harvest times below are typical. Your variety and season can shift them.

blocks.caption: When small farm crops start paying
rows: Once per planting, so plant in batches
2 to 4 weeks after transplanting, or about 2 months after planting
Leaves while the stems are still crisp
Every 2 to 3 days, on a trellis
5 to 10 days after flowering, at 10 to 12 cm long
When the seeds are half the width of a pencil
Twice a week, every 3 to 4 days

blocks.text: Leafy greens are the quickest lesson. Fruiting vegetables take longer to start, but a healthy row keeps giving for weeks. Many small farmers grow one of each, so cash comes in early and keeps coming. Our guide to [pagtatanim ng gulay](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-gulay) covers land preparation and care, and [fertilizer for vegetables](/blog/fertilizer-for-vegetables-philippines) covers feeding.

blocks.title: Plant in batches, not all at once
blocks.text: A whole plot of pechay ready on one day floods your buyer and wilts by evening. Sow a small batch every week or two instead. Then you always have something fresh to sell, and a bad week costs you only one batch. Our [staggered planting schedule](/blog/staggered-planting-schedule) guide shows how.
Can you farm on very little land?

Yes, even in containers. In urban and home gardens, you can grow pechay in 1.5 liter plastic bottles as pots, with two seedlings in each. A soil mix of garden soil, compost and rice hull works for trays and pots.

Raising seedlings is another idea for a small space. The seedling tray method uses a mix of garden soil, organic fertilizer and carbonized rice hull. Neighbors who grow talong, kamatis or sili need healthy seedlings each season, so ask them first if they would buy.
How much can you earn from a small farm?
No honest guide can give one number. Prices swing by season, and yields depend on your soil, water and care. But you can work out your own answer before you plant, then check it after.

items.title: Estimate the harvest
items.text: Ask growers near you how many kilos a plot like yours gives. Be modest for your first season.

items.title: Check the local price
items.text: Ask buyers what they paid in your harvest month last year. Prices change from month to month, so plan with the month you will sell in.

items.title: List every cost
items.text: Seeds, fertilizer, water, trellis, sprays, transport and labor, including your own days.

items.title: Subtract and decide
items.text: If sales barely cover costs, change the crop, the timing or the buyer before you start.

items.title: Record what really happened
items.text: Write the real harvest, price and costs. That is your true answer for next season.

blocks.text: Our guide to [farm profitability](/blog/farm-profitability) shows how to count it properly.
Where can you get help to start a small farm?

items: **DA National Urban and Peri Urban Agriculture Program**: under DA Administrative Order 03 of 2022, it lists seeds of mungbean and lowland vegetables, sweet potato cuttings, organic fertilizer, plastic crates and hydroponics starter kits, plus training. Ask your city or municipal agriculture office.
**RSBSA registration**: free, and it opens other DA programs for seeds, fertilizer and soil analysis.
**ACPC Agri Negosyo Loan**: up to PHP 300,000 for an individual small farmer at 2 percent interest, with a service fee of up to 3.5 percent. It asks for a farm plan and budget.

items.q: What is the most profitable crop for a small farm in the Philippines?
items.a: It depends on your buyers, water and season, so no crop wins everywhere. Fast leafy greens bring cash quickly, while okra, sitaw, ampalaya and talong pay over many pickings. Check local prices and count every cost before you choose.
Among common vegetables, pechay is one of the quickest. You can harvest it 30 to 40 days after sowing, or as early as three weeks after planting.

items.q: Can I grow vegetables in containers?
items.a: Yes. Plastic bottles of 1.5 liters can serve as pots, with two seedlings in each. Bigger containers are better.

items.q: Is there government help for backyard and urban farming?
items.a: Yes. The DA National Urban and Peri Urban Agriculture Program lists seed distribution, organic fertilizer, plastic crates, hydroponics starter kits and training. Ask your city or municipal agriculture office how to apply.

items.q: How do I know if my small farm is making money?
items.a: Write down every sale and every cost, including your own work days, for the whole season. Sales minus costs is your profit. anee.io keeps the harvest records and, on Solo Farmer, builds a Profit Report from them.
